newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Competition drives Singapore car insurers to brink.
newsitem.headline: Competition drives Singapore car insurers to brink.

text.p: Aggressive competition in motor insurance will drive rates down to unprofitable levels as players battle for market share, the chief executive of Singapore's biggest motor insurer said on Thursday.

"The need for some companies to gain market share is making them very aggressive in pricing," Tan Kin Lian, chief executive of NTUC Income Insurance Co-operative Ltd (Income) told Reuters in an interview.

Tan said pricing decisions by the most aggressive players in the soft Singapore motor insurance market were "supported more by guesswork than by (underwriting) experience". And he warned underwriting profits for the sector could be hit as a result.

Income is the biggest motor insurer in Singapore with a 33 percent share of the private car market, worth Singapore $120 million (US$85.1 million) in premiums in 1996 -- about 73 percent of its non-life portfolio of S$166.0 million.

Tan said motor insurance was intensely competitive in 1996 and would be so through 1997 as premiums came under pressure from falling car values and a drop in new vehicle registrations, thanks to government policies discouraging car use.
Motor premiums held up well for Income in 1996 at S$120.5 million, slightly up from 1995's S$120.4 million, he said.
Results released last month for its 1996 business year showed the company's total premiums up 30 percent on 1995 to S$744.0 million.

Tan said single premium life business had done particularly well, showing a surge of 123 percent to S$184.0 million. The business had benefited from good stock market performance and low bank base rates, he said.
Single premium volume for 1997 was expected to return to more normal levels and be about 80 percent of 1996's S$184.0 million.

Income's regular life premiums, at S$394.0 million in 1996, were expected up on reforms of the Central Provident Fund state pension scheme which allow more private investment. But Tan said extra effort would be put into developing general insurance.
"We do know that we want health care insurance to be much bigger than it is now," he said.

Premium for health insurance -- classed as a general insurance -- totalled about S$13.0 million for Income in 1996, about nine percent of the company's general book and is forecast to hit S$30.0 million within five years.
Much of the growth could come from telephone selling.
Tan intends to explore first commodity products that agents find uneconomical to service, such as travel and cargo insurance.
After an initial experiment with these areas in 1996, Tan said the time was ripe for expanding telephone operations.
Personal accident and household insurances are first in line with plans already advanced for telephone sales of home insurance to people in Housing Development Board (HDB) properties.
"It will happen within the next year," said Tan.
He said the move could have a major impact on the home insurance sector as about 80 percent of Singaporeans live in HDB flats.
